utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, Madam Registrar, and good morning, Prosecution, counsel, and accused. Can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. For the record, accused Pandurevic today and tomorrow will not be present, and he has waived his right to be present, so we can proceed accordingly. For the record also, we are sitting for the first session only pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Judge Stole is still on his way to the Tribunal. He was travelling and he was delayed. So he will join us after the first session. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Haynes. And that's about it. And Ms. Nikolic, and Ms. Nikolic. Yes, Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. I think we still have to deal with the exhibits to be tendered with Witness Mirko Trivic. Mr. Thayer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning to you and Your Honours. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I believe everybody has a copy of our tender sheet. There are a number of items which were used by my friends on cross and then again on redirect so we've gone ahead and added some of those documents -- obviously there are a number of them -- to the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there any document from this list that has not yet been translated into English, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe the relevant portions that were used by Defence counsel and the Prosecution have been translated into English. I do not believe that the entire personal diary of the witness was translated into English but the relevant portions which were used were. With respect to Exhibit 219, as well, that is a rather lengthy document, memorialising meetings and other reports within the Bratunac Brigade. Again, the portion that I brought to the witness's attention is translated into English. I believe everything else has been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Any objections, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: First of all, in relation to the matter that's just been raised, could I clarify? Are the remaining parts of the diary and the brigade reports going to be translated? In other words, is it the intention of the Prosecution to tender them all or only to tender those parts that were cross-examined upon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, from what I see here, it's definitely not the entire document. If we are talking of 219. Because it's bits and pieces of it. But perhaps that answers part of Mr. Josse's question. You can answer the first part, whether you intend to translate the whole document or whether you're going to limit yourself to these pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to Exhibit 219, it hadn't been our intention to translate the entire Bratunac Brigade document; only those portions that were used with a particular witness. With respect to the diary, the answer is the same. We do intend, however, to tender the entire diary, given that the witness relied on various parts. I believe his attention was drawn to various parts in terms of establishing the date. If there are other portions that my friends feel are necessary to be translated, we can go ahead and look at getting those translated but the main portions establishing the dates and events that he recalled at the time have been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that satisfy you, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But I do have objections to two other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understood that from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, 108, Your Honour, this as far as we can see was dealt with in re-examination at page 12.026 of the transcript. The questions that my learned friend Mr. Thayer asked were objected to at the time, both by Mr. Krgovic and by Madam Fauveau, and in effect the Trial Chamber upheld the objection of the Defence and the re-examination in relation to that document was not pursued. The witness therefore didn't answer the question that he was asked and in those circumstances, we submit that the document should not be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What do you have to say to that, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, my understanding of the Court's ruling on that was that the Court had heard enough on the issue of air defence preparedness and the willingness to engage in combat with NATO should they come to the defence of UNPROFOR, reinforce UNPROFOR. The document has probative value. It is of a piece with the similar language and intent, the Prosecution would submit, contained in the other documents. We think it does have probative value. It will be helpful to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Is it the kind of document that can only be tendered with this witness, Witness 109, Trivic, or can it be tendered by or through other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it can probably be tendered through other witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- later on but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he hasn't been asked questions on this document and he hasn't offered answers on this document, why should it be tendered with this particular witness rather than reserve it for later and have other witnesses give explanations on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think in line with some of the other practice we've engaged in here, it -- we've had other witnesses with whom my friends have examined, using documents that the witness had no answer for, was unfamiliar with; yet at the same time it provides an overview or completes a picture or adds some context to an issue. We believe that similarly -- and I understand we've had this discussion before, whether that particular document was objected to by a party or not at the time, and I understand that's an operative difference for the Trial Chamber, but again I would just submit that the witness was here, we raised an issue, and this document is probative to that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So our decision on P -- 65 ter number 108 is that since it hasn't been really used with Witness 109, Mirko Trivic, it will not be admitted now. It will remain marked for identification until used with some other witness. If not, it will remain marked for identification and then it will disappear from the list. Mr. Josse, I suppose you haven't finished your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I haven't. The only other objection relates to 1499. Could I make the point first of all that I hope the Trial Chamber won't regard as too churlish, but the description is particularly pejorative in relation to this document. What my learned friend has done is he has used this particular exhibits to tender list in order to reinforce the point that he wanted to make by having this particular document admitted, and that is unnecessary and frankly unnecessarily argumentative. But leaving that observation aside, the objection is as follows: It's similar to 108. I accept it's not quite so strong. What happened here was that Madam Fauveau, at approximately page 12021 of the transcript objected to the line of questioning of my learned friend. Her objection was overruled, but ultimately Your Honour asked the witness the following: Have you seen this map before? And the witness said, "No, I haven't." And really, what the Prosecution are trying to do is to get this piece in in order to make the point in the description column on the right from a witness who knew absolutely nothing about it whatsoever, and that in our submission shouldn't be permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Your comments, Mr. Thayer? Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just two quick comments. One is we have many, many maps that have been listed on our 65 ter list of exhibits. This is the way it's described on our 65 ter list of documents. It distinguishes this map from other maps. This is General Krstic's map. These are his markings, and that is how we have described it. We can in all likelihood use this map with another witness. However, as my learned friend indicated, this issue was raised by Madam Fauveau. The witness stated he didn't have any recollection of this map. Nevertheless, we would offer it, but we understand that in line with the previous ruling of the Court, the Court may wish to wait until we have a different witness, and we certainly will accept that if that's the ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our decision on this document, 1499, 65 ter number, is that you shouldn't worry about the description because that is not something that has -- that depends on how either of you wish to have it described. We will direct -- it will be marked as a map signed by General Krstic and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other thing is that we quite agree that we should follow the same line of approach as in the previous document. We'll mark it for identification until some other witness deals with it more thoroughly or more specifically. So any further objections on any of the other documents that the Prosecution wishes to tender on the part -- by any of the Defence teams? None. The other documents are therefore so admitted. We come to the documents that the Miletic Defence team wishes to tender. There are four documents. Madam Fauveau, you don't need to address us. Any objections to the admission of any of those four documents on your part, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: None, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any of the other Defence teams wishes to contest the admissibility of these four documents? None? Have they all been translated, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, Madam Fauveau. So these four documents, P106, 107, 5D361, 6D127 are so admitted. Documents that the Gvero Defence team wish to tender? There are two, 6D127, P439. Mr. Thayer, do you wish to object to any of these two documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I just note that I think one of them has just been admitted through Madam Fauveau's list, that's all. 6D127.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Grateful for that observation. Sorry we hadn't spotted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Drina Corps order of 03/1574, that's P439, has it been translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So we are only admitting that document. And then there is the Pandurevic Defence team that wished to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we come to that, I would like to just clarify with the Gvero team. You used Prosecution 33, 6D22 and 6D82 so you are not minded to tender those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's a deliberate decision not to seek tendering. For what it's worth, Your Honour, I suspect that some if not all of those documents will in due course be tendered into evidence through another route but I can't promise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon. Thank you, Mr. Josse. We come to the Pandurevic Defence team submissions. They wish to tender 18 documents that list of which has been circulated. First of all, have these -- all these been translated already into English or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A certain number of documents has been translated. Most of them have, in fact. If there are some missing translations, we will provide a list of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The Registry will coordinate --

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Registry does have a list of documents and it's quite clear on that list what has been translated and what hasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The registrar will coordinate with you and we will then know which ones have not yet been translated, in which case they will be marked for identification pending translation thereof. Any objections on your part, Mr. Thayer, for the admission of any of these 18 documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President. Just one observation with respect to -- and I'm going off of the prior exhibit list. We don't have an actual tender list. It's number 24, the interview with Momir Nikolic. I don't know whether the intention of my friends is to introduce the entire interview or just the statement portion which I believe referred to a date of a meeting. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So for the time being I have no objection as long as we are solely dealing with those portions that my friend may have referred to on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My understanding is without.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I just wanted to make sure. The other thing -- sorry to--

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Things may have changed, Mr. President, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa, I think you need to clarify this. We are talking of 7D550. Do you wish to tender the entire interview or only the relevant part that you made use of in the course of your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevant parts that we used in the course of examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Thayer, do you have an objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: None, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Any of the other Defence teams wish to object to the tendering of this or any other of the Pandurevic documents? We hear none. So one further confirmation from you. We have a note here that 7D550 and 7D551 should be in e-court today. Madam Registrar, are they in e-court already now or not yet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know whether you have put them in e-court, Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are not. We have been quicker, Mr. Sarapa. Not yet. So please try to make sure that they are in e-court without any further delay, especially since they are being admitted. So all the documents on the Pandurevic list, that's 18 of them, are being admitted. Thank you. And any other Defence team wishes to tender any other document with Witness Trivic? None. So that concludes the Trivic testimony. We now move to the next witness, unless you have any preliminaries that you wish to deal with. Mr. McCloskey is just replacing Mr. Thayer. Usher, I think you can bring the next witness in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we hold off with the witness for one second, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just a brief preliminary before the witness comes in, sorry, if we could. So I don't forget, Mr. President, if we could have a caution for this witness. I have explained to him that situation. But the preliminary I wanted to mention, as you know, I wasn't in court on Thursday, and there is an issue that I've been speaking with my colleagues from the Defence about and that I wanted to clarify with the Court because I think there was some -- a bit of confusion on both sides that I believe we've cleared up. But the Defence counsel and the Prosecution many months ago, having your rules in mind about when we needed to turn over -- when the parties needed to turn over documents used for cross-examination, we had agreed among ourselves that the appropriate time to turn over materials to be used in cross would be better at that period of time right before the cross was to begin. And there may have -- and that was our understanding that we've been going on. And there has been a bit of confusion. I've spoken to the Popovic team and they acknowledge now and are a part of that agreement. So that's the agreement we are under, as long as that's okay with the Court. That's the way we've been going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. I trust that this is clear now between the parties. Our position is very simple. We leave you to let you to come on -- to an agreement on these, and the least time we waste, court time we waste on these matters, the better it will be. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I believe that this is not really the right time to put such a request before the Trial Chamber, bearing in mind that a significant number of Prosecution witnesses have already been heard in keeping with the rules you set at the beginning of the trial. We observed on that procedure and we believe that this now opens the door to the Prosecution to announce their future witnesses in a different way. Sorry, documents, I mean. Let me correct myself. It leaves the possibility to the Prosecution to announce differently the documents they will be using in cross-examining Defence witnesses, so I don't think this is the right time to change these rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not waste time on this, Mr. Zivanovic. We've had this trial going on, proceeding smoothly, since August of last year. To my knowledge, there has only been one, two, sporadic instances. Let's proceed along the lines that we have been proceeding. There has been cooperation between the parties, more or less. If there are problems, we will encounter them, just like we did last week but I don't think there is reason for wasting more of our court time, precious court time. The witness is on his way, I hope, unless he has followed the Stankovic trail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He was in the room a few minutes ago, so I don't think he's escaped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. Can you hear me? Are you receiving interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: His microphones are switched off. So let's hear your voice again. Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How do you wish to be addressed? As General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any way you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will address you as General. So I wish to welcome you here to this case, to this trial on behalf of the Trial Chamber. Later on, we will be joined by the fourth Judge in this trial, who couldn't be with us for the first session. You're about to start giving evidence, and before you do so, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of the declaration -- solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking that you will be testifying the truth. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. Take a seat. Very soon Mr. McCloskey will be starting with his series of questions to you, but before you start testifying, since you were involved in the events, you lived through the events that are the subject matter of this trial, at least in part, it is our responsibility to draw your attention to a particular rule that we have that spells out a right that you have as a witness. As I'm going to explain to you, it's not an absolute right. It's a relative right. But basically, what this right is all about is one's right against self-incrimination, which I'm sure you must have heard about before and which has probably been explained to you. But in case it hasn't, let me explain it to you in lay language. If, in the course of your examination-in-chief or, for that matter, also upon cross-examination, any question is put to you which, if answered truthfully by you, might tend to incriminate you, then you may object to answering such question. Your objection should be addressed to us, the Judges, and we have two options. We may agree with your objection and dispense you, exempt you, from answering such question on the basis that such answers might incriminate you. Alternatively, we may decide not to entertain your objection and compel you to answer such question. This is why I have said that this right is not an absolute one. However, if we compel you to answer such questions, such incriminating questions, you have a further right. In that case, anything that you would state because you are compelled to answer such questions shall not be used as evidence in any subsequent proceedings against you for any offence except if we are talking of perjury. In that case, this further right doesn't apply any further. Have I explained this right clearly to you or have you understood me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, General. I think we can now proceed. Mr. McCloskey will go first. He's got some questions for you. I don't expect you to finish -- I don't expect to finish with your testimony today. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, General. And can you first tell us your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Manojlo Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll get into this in a bit more detail later but can you just tell us, to begin with, what your position was during 1993, 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was the chief of the Main Staff of the VRS, and I was also the deputy commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And after the war, did you -- were you appointed to any political positions?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the war, after the implementation of the Dayton Accords, the Main Staff was replaced and I was put at the disposal of the VRS for the first six months, and then for the next six months I was put at the disposal of the army of Yugoslavia. In 1998, in January of that year, I was appointed the Minister of Defence of Republika Srpska. I remained in that position up to the month of March, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. As you know, your words are being interpreted and I can tell from the interpretation that the interpreter is having to hurry a bit. So it's a bit unnatural, but try to slow your pace a bit, if you could, please. And I'll try to do the same. All right. Let's just start out with a brief personal background. Can you tell us where you were born and raised?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 21st November, 1943, in the village of Laminci in the municipality of Gradiska, both in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I did not grow up there, however. Until I was 16 I lived in my native village. There I finished the first four years of the primary school and the second part of my primary education, I did in Nova Topola near Gradiska. After completing primary school, I applied first to attend agricultural school, but because of some family problems I could not attend that school, and then I applied for the school for non-commissioned officers of the JNA. I was admitted and I completed that school in 1961.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So when you completed your military school in 1961, what rank did you graduate with?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was a Sergeant and I was assigned to duty in the Benkovac garrison near Zadar. I stayed there for some 14 months and then I applied to attend the military academy in Belgrade. I started education in October 6, 1962, and I completed in September, 1966.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you give us a brief -- and I know this could be a -- very lengthy, but if you could give us just a brief outline of your military career, when you first finished up as -- and became an officer, up until the beginning of hostilities in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Upon the completion of the military academy, where I was a very good student, I had the right to choose my garrison and I chose Banja Luka. In Banja Luka I spent the time between 1966 and 1975, I was the commander of the 10th platoon, the tank company, the reconnaissance company; then I was the commander in the class in the school for non-commissioned officers and I was also the chief of the school of reserve officers between 1973 and 1975. In 1975 I was sent for continuous education to the so-called higher military academy, which is now known as the General Staff tactics school which lasted for two years. I completed that in 1977. Upon the completion of that school, I was sent to serve in the Prilep garrison in Macedonia. I was the commander of the anti-armour battalion and I stayed there for four years in that position. In 1981, at the beginning of that year, to be more precise, on the 7th of January, I was sent to the Titov Veles garrison. A motorised brigade had been established there, the 212th motorised brigade, and I was appointed the chief operative officer in that brigade. I stayed in that position up to 1986. That year, I was sent to the command staff school for operations in Belgrade. You could call this a war school. It lasted for a year. I completed it in 1987 and then I went back to the Titov Veles garrison where I was appointed commander of the 212th Brigade. And I was also the garrison commander. I stayed in that position up to January, 1989, and then I was transferred to the command of the 3rd Army in Skoplje, and I held the position of the chief of the operations division in the operations and education organ. I stayed there until the events that took place in the territory of the former Yugoslavia up to March 1992, when I was appointed chief of the operations and education organ, which was a position occupied by a general, and I stayed there until the moment the agreement was signed for the withdrawal of the JNA from Macedonia and I was one of the main members of the team for the withdrawal of the JNA, pursuant to an agreement between the leadership of Macedonia and the General Staff of the JNA, according to which the JNA was to withdraw without a bullet being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that was, that the JNA withdrew from Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The JNA started withdrawing in February, 1992, and it was completed when the command of the 3rd Army withdrew from Skoplje to Nis, and that was on the 9th of March, 1992. And as of that date, the JNA withdrew completely from Macedonia. We did this without a single bullet fired. And that's how a war in Macedonia was avoided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you continue that brief outline leading up to your position with the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: When the JNA withdrew from Macedonia, the command of the 3rd Army was deployed in the Nis garrison. This is where I stayed for five weeks, from the 9th of March up to the 11th of May, 1992. I occupied a position of the chief of that operations and education organ and I was the acting Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army, because the assigned Chief of Staff had not arrived from Banja Luka, where he was in command of the 5th JNA Corps. I believe that he arrived either on the 18th of March or the 21st of March. He rested for sometime, and that's why I was the acting Chief of Staff of the army during that period. On the 8th of May, 1992, I got an order of the still functional Presidency of the SFRY, i.e., the supreme command of the armed forces of Yugoslavia, to be transferred from the Nis garrison to the Sarajevo garrison and to occupy the same position I had occupied in the Nis garrison. Together with that order, I also received an order by which I was appointed a General Major. I was supposed to execute that order on the 11th of May and that's when I was supposed to report to the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, in order to receive the originals of those orders and to be sent to Sarajevo. However, in the meantime, there had been some changes. As a result of that, when I arrived in Belgrade I reported to the chief of the personnel. I believe that was General Ljubojko Krstic who informed me about some changes that had happened to these orders. What was it all about? In the meantime there had been an accident in Dobrovoljacka Street in Sarajevo when the command of the 2nd Army came under attack while withdrawing from Sarajevo. Whatever remained of that army withdrew in haste. That's why I was told not to go to Sarajevo because the command of the 2nd Army no longer existed in Sarajevo, but to go to Han Pijesak to which the command had withdrawn. The second modification to the order was this: Before that, an agreement was reached between the rump Presidency of Yugoslavia and the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. According to that agreement, the JNA was to stay in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the next five years, up to 1997, and it was to equally protect the three majority populations in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was to prevent any conflicts, and when you say protection, you know what that means. The JNA was supposed to play a tampon zone role between the peoples who were in conflict. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I appreciate that, but could we try to keep to your outline of your position and of course you can explain anything you need to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can he give a date to this agreement between the Presidency of Yugoslavia and the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you exactly when this happened, but I believe that it was in March, sometime in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry to have interrupted, but can you tell us how your position evolved during these events?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was just going to tell you about that. The next modification, the third modification to the order, was as follows: Pursuant to the first order, General Ratko Mladic, after having occupied the position of the commander of the Knin Corps of the JNA, was to be appointed the Chief of Staff of the 2nd Army in Sarajevo and I was going to be appointed the chief of operations and education organ. However, on the 11th of May, an alteration was made to this effect: General Kukanjac was removed from the position of the commander of the 2nd Army to be replaced by General Mladic, and I was appointed as the Chief of Staff of the 2nd Army. I objected to that and I asked the general to whom I was talking, why I was being sent to Bosnia, i.e., to Sarajevo, knowing the JNA was in the process of withdrawal and it was disappearing from Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was told to go to Han Pijesak, to report to General Mladic, who was supposed to brief me. I arrived in the afternoon, i.e., in the evening, in the place called Crna Rijeka, nine kilometres to the east from --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you first arrive in Crna Rijeka, if you haven't told us already?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Around 11.00 on the 11th of May, 1992, and I was waiting for General Mladic, who arrived late in the afternoon. I don't know how late it was. There, in addition to General Mladic, I found ten more people. There was a total of 12 of us, four generals, Mladic, Gvero, Djukic and myself. And there were eight colonels, lieutenant colonels -- in any case, in the evening there were 12 of us there. General Mladic briefed us. He told us that the 2nd Army was being transformed, that on the following day the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Banja Luka would make a decision on the establishment of the army of Republika Srpska and that we had been appointed as members of the Main Staff. Mladic would be its commander, I would be its chief, General Gvero would be assistant commander for moral guidance, Djukic would be the assistant commander for logistics or the rear, as we called it at the time. The staff was organised with seven assistant commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I don't want to go into detail on this but can you just name the -- not -- the people, if you can, and the positions of assistant commanders, and I know you've already done that for Generals Gvero and Djukic. What were the other positions as you recall them and if you know the names at that time?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can try, but I don't know whether I will be able to follow your scheme. We shall see. The chief of the staff sector was myself. I was the chief of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army. I remained in that position throughout the war, up to 23 December 1996. The assistant commander for moral guidance, religious issues and legal issues was General Milan Gvero. The chief of sector and also the assistant commander for logistics was Djordje -- General Djordje Djukic. The assistants of intelligence and information sector was Colonel Zdravko Tolimir. The operations --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me. Let me just interrupt you. It was translated to me that General Tolimir's position was intelligence and information. Could you just repeat what your understanding was of General Tolimir's position and --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This expression intelligence and information is not correct. Tolimir was the chief of intelligence and security sector. He had two administrations and within that sector he had the information sector and the security sector or the intelligence and security sector. Petar Salapura was the intelligence chief and the security chief was Colonel Ljubisa Beara, who joined the Main Staff sometime in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And those are the -- well, are there any other assistant commanders that you can recall, the position?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The chief for the organisation, mobilisation and personnel matters was Colonel Mico Grubor, later on General. He got retired in August, 1994 and was replaced by General Petar Skrbic and stayed in that position until the end of the war. The next administration was the administration for finances and budget headed by Colonel at the time, later on General Stevo Tomic. And there was also the administration for air force and anti-aircraft Defence headed by General Jovo Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you again just briefly tell us when you first met General Mladic and what -- how well you knew him before the war?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I met with General Mladic for the first time in 1977 when I went to Macedonia. At the time, he was working in Kumanova. I don't know what position he held but we met at some manoeuvres and we stayed together in Macedonia for the next 15 years. We occupied very similar positions in the war school. We were the same generation in that war school. And we both commuted from Macedonia and back, and during the -- that one year of education, we got better acquainted. After that, Mladic was appointed commander of the 39th Infantry Division in the Stipa [phoen] garrison and I was appointed commander of the 212th motorised brigade in the Velez garrison. The distance between the two garrisons is 48 kilometres. We cooperated as brigade commanders. And then, on the same day, which I believe was the 30th of January, 1989, we were both transferred to the command of the 3rd Military District. I became the chief of the operations administration and Mladic became the chief of the education administration, which means we belonged to the same organisation of the command in the 3rd Army. We cooperated very closely as up to the second half of the year 1990, when Mladic was transferred to the Pristina garrison to the 52nd Corps of the JNA. He was the assistant commander of logistics at the time. We got separated, but then we were rejoined on -- in Crna Rijeka on that 12th of May. We knew each other very well even before the Main Staff was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know if General Mladic played a role in you becoming the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe so. And during my service in Macedonia, Mladic and I had a lot of professional conflicts, although we were friends, which means we socialised out of work, but on the job our opinions were different, and on the 11th of May, when he informed me that I would be the chief of the Main Staff and also his deputy, I was a bit startled and I had misgivings about our future cooperation, given the fact that we did not really cooperate very well while we were both in service in Macedonia. He told me only six months later what had happened. He told me, "I took you because I am very quick tempered and your reactions are somewhat slower and we would work well, both as a team." He wanted our two mentalities, two characters, to complement each other in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And again can you briefly describe to us how you worked together throughout the wartime period with General Mladic? How would you describe your ability to work with him and how well did you get along?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the very beginning, the positions of the staff sector, including my position as the head of that sector, was analysing, planning and operations, which means as follows: The staff sector, i.e., myself, prepared proposals for the commander, in this case General Mladic, on how to use the army of Republika Srpska as a whole and how to use its units, i.e., corps in various locations and at various times. The system of the work of the staff was by way of collegiums, i.e., everyday meetings. Usually all the assistants prepared proposals pertaining to their respective areas and I prepared proposals for the combat use of the units. It was very rare for Mladic not to accept my proposals, and when he made his final decisions on the item tasks for the units, he would only say, upon the proposal of the Chief of Staff. And this lasted throughout the whole time up to the end of 1994. Then I was sent westwards to the western front in Bosanska Krajina. That's when the Bihac operation took place, and that was the first time we were separated for any longer time. Upon the completion of that operation I was transferred from the Bihac front to the Glamoc front, which means I stayed in the west of Bosnia. Our separation was as prolonged. We contacted by the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. You've jumped to a description of your job, which is fine. We needed that. But what I'm after here, and just briefly is, throughout the war period, did you have any problems with General Mladic and, if not, can you describe your working relationship generally. Then we'll get into some more of the details a little bit later.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have any problems, at least not in the form of conflicts. The only thing is that General Mladic was the kind of man who even when you do something well, he always finds something wrong with it, why wasn't it faster, why weren't the losses smaller, why so many resources were expended. But that was normal for a commander. So that there was no personal conflict between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you want to keep with the original schedule?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Only because of the redactions. Otherwise we would have it 20. If that is possible, we'll try to make up for some of the lost time. Incidentally, just for public consumption and for the record, we started late this morning, not because of our -- any shortcoming on the part of anyone, but it's only because there was a technical problem with the computers of some of the Defence teams that needed to be addressed. So we'll have a short break of 20 minutes, I'm told, after which we'll reconvene. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, now we -- Judge Stole has joined us, so we are not sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis any longer. Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, General, can you tell us briefly -- we are still a bit in the background section. Can you tell us what you know of the history of -- between General Mladic and General Gvero, where they first met each other and/or worked together?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know when they first met, ever. They started to work together on that 11th of May, 1992, when we were all gathered in Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know whether they worked together and knew each other before that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: They probably knew each other because Mladic graduated from a number of military schools, just like I did, and Gvero had served some of his time as a lecturer in one of those schools, which is where I first met him myself, in 1971 or 1972. So I don't know about their history before their arrival at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us when Mr. Miletic -- I believe he was a Colonel at the time -- when he first joined up with the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Miletic arrived at the Main Staff, I believe, in the second half of July, 1992, and he was appointed to the administration of air force and air defence, to serve under General Maric, and I believe he was Chief of Staff of rocket and artillery units of the air defence. He served in that position, I don't know exactly how long, but as soon as he arrived, he displayed a certain inclination towards operative work and he often helped me because his own institution was not very busy. We didn't use our air force that much, and the systems of air defence were mainly detached across various units, and he was inclined to help me because the Main Staff was always understaffed. Our highest level of staffing was 36 per cent in all that time. So every person did two or three jobs at the same time. I singled him out as a very good staff officer, as a very good operations man, so we soon transferred him from that administration of rocket artillery units to the operations department. He was first deputy chief of operations under Dragutin Ilic, and when that man retired, Miletic took over as chief of operations in July, 1993, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you briefly describe his advancement in that position or promotions?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he arrived at the Main Staff as Lieutenant Colonel. He knows better than I do when he was promoted into Colonel but I believe it was in 1993, and he received the rank of General on the 28th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, you have briefly described your position as Chief of Staff and making proposals to the commander for the use of the army. Can you tell us a bit more detail what staff officers did you have working under you? Now, you've mentioned operations, so you may want to start there but can you tell us what the staff was made up of? And I'm really more interested now in 1995 than I am in the earlier years so if you could concentrate our answers to the year 1995. What staff units did you have that answered to you as Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I as Chief of Staff had under me only two persons on the staff, General Miletic, as chief of operations and training, and the chief of the training section, but since I stood in frequently for the commander when he was absent, the other six assistant commanders also reported to me. Not much reporting is involved, as far as the Chief of Staff is concerned. Reporting is done to the commander normally. But in the commander's absence, I received the reports. But I must say that in end 1994, and almost all of 1995, with the exception of a very few days, I was absent from the Main Staff. I was at the so-called forward command post in Drvar, Glamoc, Mrkonjic or maybe Banja Luka so I was not directly participating in the work of the Main Staff in Crna Rijeka although I continued officially to be Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We'll get into that in a bit. Can you describe the job of chief of operations? What was Miletic's job, especially in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: General Miletic's job in 1995 was more of a technical staff nature. Whatever the commander decided, Miletic translated into documents, orders, notices, briefs, depending on what the commander wanted. If the commander conceived a military operation in any part of the theatre of war, he would notify Miletic and give him guidelines reflecting his wishes, and Miletic then translated that into documents. So he was a writing man. He translated the commander's words onto paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, what was he involved in in terms of the operations that he was involved in, overseeing? Once Mladic decided on a particular operation, what did the chief of operations -- what was his normal involvement? Surely it was more than just being involved in paper.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In my absence, Mladic was not able to -- in fact, it was not appropriate for him to send Miletic to the front line to conduct or control any of the military operations. Miletic would always stay behind in staff headquarters, especially when both Mladic and I were absent and that was a frequent occurrence in 1995. As far as I know, in 1995, Miletic did not leave the Main Staff, although of course he's better placed to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it important to have a trusted general at the Main Staff headquarters overseeing operations from that level?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the general who would remain at the Main Staff, be it Miletic or myself, was a person receiving incoming information from theatres of war, analysing that information and suggesting solutions to the commander for any possible problems. That is the person who is the hub of all incoming information from various theatres of war. He brings to the command's notice any problems that may have occurred, and practically, I don't know how to put it but that's the main -- operator of the information switchboard. He distributes information across various sectors, depending of what is relevant to whom, receives proposals and suggestions from subordinate commanders, wraps them up and gives them a certain shape and transmits them to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what is his -- his responsibility in implementing the commander's orders? The chief of operations in this case, General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He has no responsibility for the execution of orders in the field. His only responsibility is to accept reports from subordinates and to transmit them to the commander. It is not up to him to do anything with an order signed by the commander except to send it to the corps to which it was intended. And then through daily reports, he monitors the course of execution of that order and informs the commander on whether it's going according to plan or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when it's not going to plan, would he be the person that passed on the orders or the -- of the commander to clear up the problem? Or would you? Who would do that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: If something is not going according to plan, or, rather, order, then Miletic or I, if I am there, would inform the commander of the problem, and at the same time we could also suggest a solution but the final decision of course is up to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me -- before we go any deeper into this -- ask you just a basic question about the rules of the VRS. Did you adopt any particular set of rules from any particular army, as you got off the ground in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. All armies, all the three armies in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Muslim, the Croat and the Serb army, inherited most, if not all, the rules of the former JNA because those were the rules according to which we had been trained. They were the only rules we knew. And we just adjusted them to specific situations or specific needs of the VRS. Thus, for instance, in August, 1992, when the army was just established, we created a so-called temporary rule of service of the VRS. In fact, we selected certain details from the rule of service of the JNA and adjusted them to the needs of the VRS, reducing the original size from 360 pages to 43 pages or something. I believe I gave this to the OTP sometime in 2001. As for rules of engagement, we applied the rules of engagement of the former JNA but only in the measure in which the size of units corresponded. For instance, we had some light infantry brigades and some motorised brigades, who were much smaller than similar units in the JNA. For instance, an infantry brigade in the JNA had 5500 men, and in the VRS, it had 1500 or so, rarely 3500. So we took over from the JNA practically all rules of conduct. The only difference was that we didn't make any bones about that. We didn't make any bones about that, unlike all the other armies who wanted to have nothing to do with the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us, in your job, did you have any responsibilities relating to materials like ammunition and fuel and other valuable commodities?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The responsibility of the logistics sector was to procure all equipment and materials necessary for the war. Now, there is a group of materials, such as strategic materiel, that's munitions and weapons, fuel, food, clothing and footwear. Those are the basic needs without which you can't wage war. Now, the logistics sector -- or, rather, the responsibility for distributing this material lay with the Chief of Staff, that is me. Now, for instance, General Djukic, that is the logistics sector, procures, let's say, a million rounds for a rifle. He was not able to distribute that across units, so I made the decision, the list, depending on the size of corps, depending on the tasks they were performing, I would say, "You'll give 300.000 rounds to the 1st Corps." To the 2nd Corps, which was passive for the first three years of war, I would give only a minimum, just enough to fill the combat set, as it was prescribed. That was one combat set. To the Drina Corps which was constantly involved in one operation or another, I would give 200.000 rounds. It would sometimes happen that I gave nothing to certain corps because there were no combat activities for them. And the same went for fuel. Fuel and munitions were short. And, for instance, when the logistics sector got hold of, let's say, 1.000 tonnes of fuel, I would apply the same criteria to distributing fuel as I applied to distributing ammunition. As for other strategic materiel such as food, clothing and footwear, I didn't meddle in that much, although it was officially my responsibility, for the simple reason that every soldier, whether he was waging war actively or not, had to be clothed and fed. And I left it to the quartermaster of the logistical sector to deal with the distribution. The only thing that was taken into account was the number of soldiers in a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let me jump over and ask you another structural question. Can you just briefly describe to us what the 65th Protection Regiment was and where it fit into the structure of the VRS, just very briefly? We don't need too much detail on this.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose of the 65th Protection Regiment, motorised regiment, was to provide security for the Main Staff. On its strength, as far as I can remember, it had a battalion of the military police, a motorised combat battalion, its own sabotage unit linked up with the 10th Sabotage unit of the Main Staff. I may have omitted a less important unit but in any case, this was the main purpose of the Protection Regiment. Since the Protection Regiment was an elite unit, predominantly consisting of troops who were doing their regular service and very few reservists, very often that regiment would be used as a reserve for the Main Staff, for interventions in the areas where we were not doing so well. The regiment would often be split into two. Half of the troops would be with the Main Staff and the other half would be somewhere on the front line. We did not often need it for the physical security of the Main Staff because there was a signals regiment who stayed with the Main Staff all the time. In addition to their main purpose which was signals maintenance, they were also trained to participate in combat and to provide security for the Main Staff, which we often used whenever necessary, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who in the Main Staff was responsible for the 65th Protection Regiment? Where did it fit into the structure?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The regiment commander was directly subordinated to the commander of the Main Staff. If the regiment was engaged in the defence of the Main Staff, which happened on three or four occasions throughout the war, then its commander would have been the most senior general in the Main Staff, and that was me more often than not, but this was only applied to the area where the Main Staff was employed -- deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And who was the commander of the 65th Protection Regiment in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Milanmir [phoen] Savicic. He was in command of that regiment throughout the entire war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just can you say the name again? It didn't -- we didn't quite get it.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Milomir Savicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. And for the 10th diversionary unit, can you describe what its function was and where it fit into the Main Staff structure?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The 10th diversionary detachment was established towards the end of 1992 or the beginning of 1993. I know it was winter. I can't remember exactly when it was. It was trained at the time. It was first billeted at Vlasenica, that's where it was trained. It was used to collect information and intelligence on the enemy. It would infiltrate behind enemy lines. It was also used for anti-sabotage operations and also for the defence of the Main Staff, if there happened to be there in the vicinity. This was a very small but elite unit. I know that in the first group that we trained, there were not more than 53 men. That detachment suffered constant losses all the time. The last time I was in contact with that detachment, they had only 24 men. This was sometime in July or August, 1993. I don't know how it was replenished after that and how its strength evolved after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who did it fall under or -- in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you interviewed me in Banja Luka, I made a mistake. I told you that the person in charge was the security organ. However, the person in charge of its use was subordinate to the intelligence service of the Main Staff, which was headed by Colonel Petar Salapura. The ultimate person in charge was General Tolimir, who was the chief of the intelligence and security sector. I told you in Banja Luka that it was the security administration that was in charge and I did that, I made a mistake, because I had only one occasion to issue an order to that detachment during the Lukavac 93 operation. The order was received by General Tolimir and he went to Han Pijesak to execute the order, to move the detachment. In the meantime, he had suffered a stroke and in his notebook, this mission was found as having been recorded. Colonel Beara, the chief of security administration, came to me and I issued a task to him. And based on that, I told you in Banja Luka that it was the security administration that was in charge of the sabotage activities of that unit, which is not the case. It was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that clarification. Now, you've mentioned twice that you've issued orders, and I don't need to get into the Lukavac 93 situation but can you explain, were you actually issuing orders or were these orders that you had passed on from your commander, General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Lukavac 93 operation had been planned by the staff sector, i.e., myself. During the execution of that operation, and during the stage of the preparations on the ground from Visegrad to Ustipraca lasted for some month and a half. However, officially, the operation to liberate Trnovo or the Lukavac 93 operation started on the 6th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't want to get into the details of it. Can you just tell us how it was you, as the Chief of Staff, could issue orders for that operation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The witness said at the beginning of his testimony that he had a dual function. He was the Chief of Staff and he was the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why would that be an objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the Prosecutor is now asking him how come that he, as the Chief of Staff, was in a position to issue any orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm asking him to -- so he can specifically describe what his position was at that time, so it can be clarified. And when I say Chief of Staff I'm referring to generally that was his job. Perhaps he was acting commander then. Perhaps he was deputy commander. Perhaps he was passing on orders. I mean there is several possibilities here and I think the witness can answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then you can rephrase the question, omitting the description of Chief of Staff and just ask him in relation to the Lukavac 93 operation whether he was in a position to issue orders, and if so, in what capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's my understanding that he is always Chief of Staff, so I don't want to leave the impression that he would not have been Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he can answer the question. Let's proceed. Could you issue orders in relation to the Lukavac 93 operation, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In what capacity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the operation commander. I was in command of the Sarajevo Corps, the Drina Corps, and the reinforcement of the two corps, four brigades from other corps, the Krajina Corps and some from the East Bosnia Corps. General Mladic had decided that I should be in charge of the operation. The operation started as I've already told you, on the 6th of July and General Mladic was with me from the morning. The operation started at 6.00. He was with me until 10.00 or thereabouts and then he told me, "Chief, I am leaving to have some rest. You know where I'll be. You carry on with the operation," and I continued until the 11th of July, which means that I had the right to command over all units that found themselves in the area and I've already told them which units those were. On the 11th of July, we entered Trnovo. In the afternoon the commander arrived. He took over the command, and he sent me to what he called at the time a well-deserved four-day furlough. I returned to Han Pijesak and rested and the commander continued carrying out the operation. In other words, before he came, I had an absolute right of command in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And General, is it appropriate under the JNA rules and under the VRS rules for a commander to appoint someone like yourself or someone else as a temporary commander, thereby giving him the command responsibilities of a commander?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was possible pursuant to the JNA rules and pursuant to our own rules, but not -- it does not apply to the entire military or to entire theatre of war but only to some sectors of the theatre of war. Such was the case for example, during the Lukavac 93 operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I want to go from Lukavac 93, the Trnovo, to the situation in the Krajina, when, I think, the VRS was anticipating an offensive in that area, and were you appointed any kind of command role to deal with the upcoming offensive, I think what's been known now as Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question. Operation Storm is -- was a Croatian operation and ours was a defence operation. What period are you referring to? Are you referring to the year 1995 or to some other period?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that was an awkward question. I am referring to operation -- to 1995, and I wanted to know what position you were appointed to, if any, in dealing with the Croatian offensive.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The situation was very similar as in the Lukavac 93 operation. The problem started towards the end of 1994, to be more precise, in October. The 5th Muslim Corps on the 23rd October 1994, with some 22.000 troops, left the secure area of Bihac and attacked the Serb positions on the right bank of the river Una. The attack was sudden, very quick. We had not expected that somebody would dare leave the security area, where nobody was allowed to carry arms, and we did not expect anybody to attack from there. They did that, and in the next seven days they took over some of the Serb territories around Grmec, about 250.000 square kilometres in size. At the session of the Supreme Command on the 28th of October, or a night later, which was held at the command of the Main Staff and was attended by the president of the republic as the Supreme Commander, one of the vice-presidents and I believe -- not that I believe. I know that it was Nikola Koljevic and Mr. Krajisnik, who was the speaker of the assembly, the then-president of the government whose name was Kosic, and I don't know his first name, and the inner circle of the Main Staff. We discussed the situation during the night and at 4.00, the Supreme Commander decided upon the proposal of the commander of the Main Staff that I should go west to Grmic will have to establish what had happened and what was going on there. I told them that I knew what was going on because we received daily combat reports from the area. However, I told them if I was to go there, I wanted to take a few more officers along and try and do something, not only to establish what the situation was. I even set some conditions. I told them that if I were to do something, the Supreme Command, before I arrived in the area, should at least for the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps, proclaim the state of war, because we had never proclaimed a state of war, whereas the Muslims and Croats had done that on the 4th of August, 1992. They waged their war pursuant to the rules of war and customs of war which we didn't do. The second condition was that I should be placed at my disposal the reserve of the Main Staff which was the centre of military schools in Banja Luka, and also, that I should be given two or three brigades from the other corps, depending on what troops could be assigned to me. On my travel towards mount Grmic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. Were you placed in command for this situation, like you had been for the Trnovo operation?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say that I was placed in command. I was ordered to stop the Muslim offensive and, if possible, to launch a counterattack. This type of order actually put at my disposal the troops of the 2nd Krajina Corps which was withdrawing at that time, and newly brought forces. I was even given two brigades from the Republic of Srpska Krajina, from the army of Srpska Krajina. That's how I became the commander of some joint Serb forces in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's jump briefly, then, to July -- well, the spring and July of 1995. Were you involved in that command during those-- during that period?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Upon the completion of the Bihac operation, which was towards the end of December, to be more precise on the 25th of December, I was transferred. The so-called Carter's four-month period had come into effect in the Bihac region. In the southeast --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, sorry, was that December what year?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: 1994. I was transferred to the Glamoc theatre of war because the Croats had launched a small-scale offensive from the Livanjsko field towards Glamoc and Grahovo. In practical terms, I again took over the command of the 2nd Corps. Since the situation around Bihac was calm and was conserved I took several units, I believe two or -- brigades and I took them with me to the general area of Glamoc. In practical terms, nothing changed. I still had the right to command over those forces in Western Bosnia. And this lasted with short interruptions when I came to the Main Staff in March, and finally on the 29th of May, I went to the area and I got engaged in a defence operation against the Croatian Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And that's the operation I'm interested in. From the 29th of May, were you in command of that defence operation against the Croatian Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, when you are taking on the important responsibilities of command, especially in such an important operation, can you tell us, did you still retain your position as Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you're going to be commanding this important operation, what person or persons would have taken over your important duties at the headquarters as the Chief of Staff, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Main Staff, when I was absent from the Main Staff, it was the most senior in the staff sector, which at the time was General Miletic. He would take over from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So during that time you were dealing with Operation Storm, was it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Madam Fauveau. Sorry to interrupt you, but Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation] -- [Interpretation] ... in the lines 9 to 11, two words are missing because the witness said that those were regular every day jobs and the most senior in the staff would take over the routine every day jobs, and this is what we are missing in the transcript. I would like this to be corrected. This is the second sentence from [In English] [Microphone not activated], it should say, "he took over routine, everyday duties from me." This is what the sentence should read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, would you accept that what Ms. Fauveau has just stated, does it reflect what you actually had stated yourself? And I'm asking you for the purposes of the transcript more than anything else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say that Miletic was the most senior after me in the staff. I said that he was the most senior officer in the staff's sector. In the staff, there were several other sectors that I mentioned at the beginning of my testimony. In other words, Miletic took over from me the routine daily task, which was accepting reports from the subordinates, their processing, briefing the commander, and other daily routine jobs that are normally performed by the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And thank you for that clarification. Briefing the commander is a rather important job, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the interpretation, briefing the commander, what do you mean? Are you referring to the commander receiving reports or the commander reporting to somebody, briefing somebody? What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We may have a translation issue. Your previous answer, you mentioned that one of the jobs that General Miletic took over was briefing the commander, and I was asking whether or not Miletic briefing the commander, as you put it, was that an important job?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did that briefing of the commander also extend to providing daily reports to the Supreme Commander-- the Supreme Command, excuse me, the Supreme Command, the civilian body headed by Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I know you have seen and I will show you what has been described as a daily report from the Main Staff to the Supreme Command, but can you tell us what those reports were, how often they went out?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Daily or regular combat reports of the Main Staff towards the Supreme Command went every day. They were called regular or daily combat reports. Their purpose was to inform the Supreme Command, since it was a political body, not a military one. It was simply a description of the events that took place in the past day on the battlefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of those reports?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose of the reports was for the Supreme Command, since it consisted of civilians, to be kept abreast of events on the battlefield. They were not two-way reports, and the Supreme Command had no influence on the situation in the theatre of war, unless the Supreme Commander decided to do something on the basis of those reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Mr. McCloskey. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe there is again an error in the transcript, line 13, [In English] "influence" actually should be "and the report had no influence."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So according to you, they were not two-way reports and the report to the Supreme Command had no influence on the situation in the theatre and war, is that what you mean to say, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, you have heard the exchange between me and Madam Fauveau. Do you agree to that; in other words, that the reports to the Supreme Command had no influence on the situation in the theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not, unless the Supreme Commander decided to take an action in response to a problem notified by the Main Staff. But the Supreme Command did not have any executive functions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, General. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So these daily reports were a -- were they a significant part of the information received by the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Yes, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the transcript remains the same. It's page 45, line 5 [In English] "but the Supreme Command did not have any executive functions," and actually the witness told, "but the report did not have any executive function."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I think we can proceed. That will be taken into account and we can proceed. Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Thank you for pointing it out, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These daily reports, were they considered by you to be significant information being sent to the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I did not understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was the information in these reports important for the Supreme Command to receive?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did the Supreme Command in part use the information in those reports to make their decisions?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know that. I don't know whether they used those reports to make important decisions, but occasionally the Supreme Commander or the Supreme Command did take a voice, issuing tasks to the VRS and one could conclude that they were in response to some of those reports, the reports on decisive actions such as the report on the Muslim offensive, Muslim attacks, originating from enclaves, the Croat offensive, Operation Storm, and similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps I've taken something for granted. Perhaps you could briefly explain it to us if you could. Could you tell us the authority that the Supreme Commander has over the army as designed in the political system in place at the time?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately upon the decision to establish the army on the 12th of May, 1992, following an automatic course, the then-president of the republic of -- Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Radovan Karadzic, became the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Armed forces also include the police and the so-called civilian defence. So the army is one of the components of the armed forces. Now, having received Supreme Command over the army, the Supreme Commander has directly under him the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff. However, the Supreme Command was formed in end 1992. I received that information from General Djukic on the 6th of December, and it was mainly politicians who were included in the Supreme Command, president of the republic, president of the parliament, Prime Minister, Minister of Defence and Minister of the Interior.
