It did not include, I'm talking about politicians now, the two vice-presidents and none of the members of the Main Staff. The commander of the Main Staff, that is General Mladic, should have been included in the Supreme Command automatically. Following an intervention from the Main Staff, the Supreme Command included both vice-presidents, that's Mr. Nikola Koljevic and Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, but none of the generals. We were, in fact, invited to some of the sessions of the Supreme Command but just as observers, to avoid duplicating the task of conveying assignments from the Supreme Command downwards. Usually General Mladic would go or I or one of the other generals, depending on the specific agenda for that session of the Supreme Command so as to avoid the possibility that the Main Staff would convert into a headquarters of the Supreme Command. There were parallel tracks in commanding the army. Both the commander of the Main Staff and the Supreme Commander had command of the army. Since at that time, in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which later became Republika Srpska, the one-party system prevailed, the then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. I appreciate this is a complicated subject, and it's an important subject, but can you tell us how it worked in July, 1995? I know there was developments throughout but can you just give us, if there is anything you need to add than what you've already added, but please focus on 1995.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can put this more briefly. General Ratko Mladic was immediately subordinated to the Supreme Commander, that is Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And in July, 1995, was that system working as it was designed?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In July, 1995, the system functioned in principle. Karadzic was still directly superior to Mladic but for reasons that I ignore, Karadzic started sending orders directly to me, to the western front, and again there were parallel tracks in exerting command. It was my legal obligation to execute the orders of General Mladic and only exceptionally in emergencies, to execute directly the orders of my superior commander, who is my second higher superior. Whenever I received such direct order, I was to inform Mladic immediately. Since Karadzic continued to send orders directly to me, I was duty-bound to return every such order to General Mladic and have him tell me, "Do it" or "Do not do it." And if he told me to do it, then he had to say how. I warned Karadzic, who visited the western front rather frequently at that time, that this was a duplication of command and procrastination because instead of 24 hours, an order took 48 hours to execute. However, he did not heed my words and that continued for the entire duration of the Operation Storm, until the 4th August 1995, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. But in July 1995, was there any member of the Main Staff on the Supreme Command? Or had it remained separate, as you had described earlier?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: They were separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go to one of these reports that we've been speaking of. It's number -- 65 ter number 44. That will be coming up on your screen. And this is, as we wait for it to come up, it's entitled "Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army, very urgent, to the President of Republika Srpska" and then it has various corps and other units listed as on the address sheet. And there is that part that I just read up in the left-hand corner, and if we could just -- well, let's keep it there for a second. General, is this an example of the front page of one of these reports we've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have before me a strictly confidential report, 03/3-193, dated 12th July 1995, if that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And does that look like the kind of daily report that the Main Staff sent to the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we could go over to the last page of the B/C/S, and these -- the reports basically go corps by corps and describe the situation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we just go through this report and get to the last page, if possible? Okay. That's -- that's good. And I'll just -- I want you to look, as you can, I know this looks like a teletype so there is no signature but there are initials on the report, MDJ/MM. Do you know what those initials mean or signify?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think this is MADJ. I think it's KADJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know what those initials mean or what they signify?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do, I do. Before the line, it's the indication of the author of the document. I believe it was Colonel Krsto Djeric. And after the slash, MM, those are the initials of the person who typed up the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where -- what was Krsto Djeric's position?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Krsto Djeric worked in the operations and training sector. I can't remember whether he was in training or in operations but I believe he was in training, and that's probably why General Miletic used him as an assistant, because Miletic could not handle all my work, processing reports from subordinates, writing reports to the Supreme Commander, reacting to requests from lower units and monitoring the execution of orders issued from above. Those were the things that I did as well together with Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were you from July 1st through, I believe, about September 4th, 1995? Most of the time, if I could say. I know that you weren't only in one place but most of the time, where were you during those dates?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: From 29 May until end October, 1995, I was constantly on the western front, in Drvar, at Ostrelj, at the Kula facility near Mrkonjic Grad and in Banja Luka. On the occasion of the retreat of the Serb army before the Croatian Operation Storm. I think it only happened once, on the 19th and 20th July, that I came to Crna Rijeka to attend the farewell party for General Zivanovic who was retiring and at the same time the appointment of General Krstic as commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll get into that in a bit, but on 12 July, where were you, 1995, when this report was done?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, I was at Krupa on the Una River. I remember that time very well because the night before the 12th of July, I had lost a bridge that we had been holding on the coast, on the same level as Krupa on the Una River.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then getting back to this document, at the bottom, it says under those initials, "Standing in for the Chief of Staff, Major General Radivoje Miletic." Can you tell us what that means and the significance of that, "Standing in for the Chief of Staff"? First of all, is that correct? Is that what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That word "standing in" actually means replacing. But in military terminology, and according to military rules, only one word would suffice here, "for," followed by my full name, so it would be Chief of Staff, Lieutenant Colonel General Manojlo Milovanovic and then Miletic could sign but he wrote instead, "standing in for." That's a special legal category called acting something, and that had to be regulated by an order. He could be acting for me if I was absent from the theatre of war or if I was on sick leave. But I was in the theatre of war at that time. I don't see that this is a big deal. I believe that this is an administrative error. And the initials indicating the author, as well as the teletype operator who accepted the document, because this document, like many others I've seen these days, does not have the initials of Miletic because that's something the teletype cannot convey, but the teletype operator who handled this had to put in the acronym SR standing in Serbian for svojerucno, in his own hand. That would have meant that Miletic had signed the document himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you have had a chance recently in my office to review all of the reports to the -- from the Main Staff to the Supreme Command for 1995 that are in the possession of the Prosecution, and is it fair to say that literally hundreds of those reports are in the name of General Miletic under the title, "Standing in for the Chief of Staff"?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. There were 365 reports from the 1st of January 1995 until the 31st December 1995. All of them bear the same marking, "Standing in for Chief of Staff." I found only one that is signed, but that one was probably not teletyped, it was sent either by fax or by courier, because it included Miletic's signature. So out of those 365, only one bears Miletic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But not all 365 were Miletic's name. Weren't many of them under your name as Chief of Staff as well?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, you're right. A lot of them bear my name. I didn't count them. But in the list of documents, I indicated some that I believe were not mine. I placed the word "ne," no. Against some of the others, I placed the words "possibly," but there were some that I don't remember doing as Chief of Staff. Those that I marked as "possible," you can take as my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you had a chance to sit down with this material and work with an investigator in the last couple of days to note which ones had your name and which ones had General Miletic's name on them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And that's what I did, in pencil, on that list of documents, in the part where my signatures are. As for the other documents, bearing Miletic's signature, they were in files marked green, marked with green stickers. I wrote my opinion, and I gave that to you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So when we talk about this label, "Standing in for the Chief of Staff," that same label was on those hundreds of reports that went out under Miletic's name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So was it well known to you and everyone in the Main Staff that handled these reports that General Miletic was doing this?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. When I returned to the Main Staff, or when I visited occasionally, I had no need to look up those reports because they were history. So I found about that for the first time two years ago in Banja Luka when you sent me that invitation to attend an interview. Together with that invitation or summons I received the indictment against Tolimir, Gvero and Miletic, and that's when I read the clause where it says that the documents were signed with "Standing in for Chief of Staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If you didn't know but surely the other people in the staff knew about this. I don't want to overemphasise this as I've already said it's not a great sin, but this clearly was done hundreds of times, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Having reviewed that -- those documents very -- I know -- briefly, is it -- can one make a fair conclusion that the times that General Miletic's name are on these documents is the time when he is taking over your duties in terms of this kind of responsibility, and when it's your name, you're back temporarily at the headquarters taking over this duty?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I -- you may not remember this, but I'm just noting from your -- your accounting work that you did, that you noted that from 31 May to 4 September, they were type-signed by Radivoje Miletic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the date, from which May?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 31 May to 4 September.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is true, and that is justified because I arrived in Drvar on the 29th May and I stayed there all the time up to the end October. Why is the 4th of September important? I continued my stay in the western part of Bosnia in September and in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It may not be crucially important. I'm just looking at your accounting report because it goes on to say from September 9th through 18th November, these reports were also type-signed by Radivoje Miletic. Is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I noticed that yesterday or the day before yesterday, as I was looking at the document. I saw that Miletic's signature appears on the documents dating back to the 31st of December, whereas the second half of November and the entire December I was in the Main Staff. On the 21st of November the peace agreement was signed. Still, by some sort of inertia Miletic continued to brief the Supreme Command, although combat activities had stopped, but nobody ever ordered us to stop daily briefings. I noticed that and I did find it a bit strange that this inertia procedure continued. I can't explain how this happened. I believe that the people with shortened initials continued doing their job and I suppose they didn't deem it important who would sign these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to go to some particular paragraph in this number 44 document that we have. And if in the B/C/S we could go to what's listed as number 6, entitled, "In the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps" and it would be section B, "Situation in the corps." And I think we see that up on the -- you can see the B/C/S. And I just-- I'll read briefly some of the information that is contained in this. I'll start with where it says, "Engagements of units in the execution of the Krivaja 95 task. All the combat tasks are going ahead as planned. During the day they liberated Potocari and they continue advancing in order to liberate all the settlements in Srebrenica enclave. On the blank access" -- we don't understand that word, sorry -- "part of our units and MUP units have organised ambushes in order to destroy Muslim extremists who have not surrendered and who are trying to break out from the enclave towards Tuzla." And it goes on and talks about, "In the situation of the territory, in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps, the population is being taken by organised transport from Srebrenica towards Kladanj, during the day about 10.000 Muslims are estimated for transport. In all the areas of responsibility of the corps, the situation on the territory is stable and under control. During the day, in most populated areas, recruits were being sent off to the army. All the planned and approved convoys passed safely through the RS territory." Now, can you tell us where that information that I just read, where does that come from? How is it -- who does General Miletic receive this information from?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I have an objection to the interpretation of the words under Roman II, the situation on the territory. It says here, and the sentence starts with the following words, "In the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps, from the Srebrenica enclave," and I got a somewhat different interpretation. The Drina Corps was omitted, and I got the interpretation as "in the Srebrenica enclave."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's just a problem with me reading it. We put the interpreters on the spot. The exact document is the one to make reference to. They do a good job, as you can tell, but it can never be perfect.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was not my intention to criticise the interpreters. I just wanted to draw your attention to the fact that something was read out incorrectly. Instead of "in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps," I heard it "in the area of responsibility of the Srebrenica enclave." But this is a minor point. As far as your question is concerned, how did Miletic obtain this information? I told you that on that day, I was in Krupa on the Una in the west and I really don't know, I can only assume how Miletic had obtained this information. I suppose most probably, and I repeat I only assume, he received this information from the regular combat report of the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We don't want to you speculate or -- but my question was what -- was there a normal procedure by which the corps sent this kind of information up to the Main Staff so they could choose what they needed and then send it on to the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that I have already spoken about the procedure, at least in part. This was the procedure: Every day, the corps, up to 2200 hours, sent their regular combat reports to the Main Staff. I would receive those combat reports I was in -- if I was in the Main Staff. If I was absent, they were received by Miletic. When all the combat reports arrived from all the different corps, the person who received them, either me or Miletic, would read them, and while that person was reading, as of 2000 hours the corps commanders started reporting in by telephone. Since these combat reports showed situation at different times, the battalion commander sends reports to the brigade commander around 1500 hours. The brigade commander needs about an hour to study the report and to draft his own combat report to be sent to the corps commander. The corps commander needs to study all the reports, i.e., this is done by his staff organs, and based on the brigade reports, he drafts a report to the Main Staff. The Main Staff receives that report before 2000 hours but with the situation as at 1500 hours. Five hours in combat means a lot. At 2000 hours, corps commanders report in by telephone. We had direct telephone connections. And they say whether there are any changes with respect to the combat report or not. If there are changes, then they report about the changes orally. And then General Miletic studies all the reports and separates things that are important for each sector, what is important for General Gvero, for the moral guidance, what is important for the logistics. Let me not go through all the sectors. Every morning at 7.00, there is a meeting of the Main Staff. Usually it is the inner circle which means General Mladic with all his assistants and regularly these morning meetings were attended by the chief of the operations administration, the chief of the intelligence administration, and the security administration, in addition to the assistant commanders. And it would usually be the commander, General Mladic, who would call the meeting to order and he would give the floor to the General Miletic standing in for the Chief of Staff, and then we -- either me or him would inform all the present about the problems in the theatre of war and we would draw each sector's chief to what they had to pay attention. For example, if a soldier deserted from a corps or if the corps doesn't have ammunition, we direct chiefs of sectors' attention to such things. We did not read complete reports, because this would have taken a whole day. The Main Staff would have done nothing but read reports. After the meeting, chiefs of sectors would study the details that their attention had been drawn to and that they provide proposals to the commander. Usually, it would happen immediately, during the first meeting. If there was a lot of such thing, then there would be a need for us to meet either once or even twice in the course of the same day. This was a system that was in place and based on this system, Miletic obtained this particular information. It did happen that the commander was not in the staff, the Chief of Staff was not in the staff, and then the most senior general would chair this meeting, but Miletic again was the one who explained the situation, who provided an insight into the situation based on the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see it's break time, and I know I'm well over my time. I hope to finish up in 40 minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, could we go to another document? It's 65 ter number 49, and just a quick question about something that I saw. It's another report from the Main Staff to the president of the Republika Srpska. This one is dated 15 July 1995, as you can see as it's coming up on your screen, and if we could go again to paragraph 6, the Drina Corps zone, which is page 3 of the English and we can just go into paragraph 6 of the B/C/S, page 3 of the B/C/S as well, and I wanted to ask you about -- it's in section A, and I won't go through all of it. It talks a bit about Zepa and a bit about Srebrenica -- actually, as you can see, talks about the defence lines of the 4th, 6th and 7th Battalions of the Zvornik Brigade and the trouble they were in. Then it goes on to say that during transport towards Zvornik, the Turkish troops pulling out from Srebrenica towards Tuzla opened fire on an ambulance in the Planica village sector and killed the driver of the vehicle and a paramedic. Now, as you're aware, this term "Turkish" is a term that Muslims find very offensive, as they are not ethnically Turkish, they are Slavs. And we know that wars always generate these kinds of terms that soldiers use, but why is this term -- how has this term found its way into a report at the level of the Main Staff, to the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in my view, was an attempt to complete the Second World War, so to speak. At the very beginning, and in 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm a little worried, General. I know history is important, but it's a relatively simple question and I don't want to interrupt you too much but go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau. One moment, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the question was not simple by any count, and I would like the witness to be allowed to answer the way he wants to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We tend to agree with Madam Fauveau. Let him answer. Instead of taking you 40 minutes it will take you 45 and that will complete the session for today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Go ahead, General.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: To make a long story short, let me put it this way: At the beginning of the war, we all called each other names. The Muslims and the Croats called us Chetniks. We called Muslims the Turks. And we called the Croats Ustasha. That is the way it was. I can't see the initials here. I don't know who drafted this document. But I suppose that the document was drafted by somebody who just continued that practice. However, my experience tells me that Muslims who are of Slav origin were not offended if they were called Turks because they identified themselves with Muslims of Islamic origin, whereas the Serbs were insulted by the term Chetniks, and let me not go into explaining why. And Croats equally were offended by the term Ustasha. I do not have an explanation as to how this word could find its way to the report. I suppose that one of the authors, somebody who drafted the letter -- I'm sure it wasn't Miletic, I don't know actually -- used this word "Turks," I don't know why. But there is another side to this coin and that is why somebody from the leadership or the military command did not react or maybe they did but I don't know about that. This is just my opinion, the only thing I can share with you as to how this word came into the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's go to another series of documents. I'll just ask you about one and they are called directives, something that I know we have talked about before. Can you tell us what these directives were that came from the president or General Mladic? Just generally tell us and then we'll get to a couple of them.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: These directives are documents issued by the Supreme Command. They are political documents, war policy documents, rather than anything else. They are recommendations or requests by the Supreme Command to the armed forces. And they are documents that define the axes of activities of the armed forces in a long run and they usually apply to the armed forces as the biggest part of the armed -- or of the army or of the military. The directives were drafted in the following way: The Supreme Command, through the Supreme Commander, talks to the team that is going to be in charge of the directive and gives the team guidelines, either in the written form, featuring some tasks or prospects for the army activities, or this can be orally conveyed to the commander or to the person who will be the directive team leader. That person jots down the guidelines and then drafts the directive as a document. Since our Supreme Command was not technically or in any other way equipped to deal with military issues, they did not have the necessary personnel which the Ministry of Defence had, and they were supposed to do that, this job was handed down to the Main Staff. And the authors of all these directives, maybe with one or two exceptions, the authors of all these directives were members of the Main Staff. When an author using his knowledge and capabilities drafts a directive, he sends it back to the Supreme Command as a draft. The Supreme Command then analyses it, takes out what is not necessary, adds what they deem necessary, and with certain remarks and notes, they return it to the author. The author then enters all the corrections, as ordered, comes up with a final version. That is again returned to the Supreme Commander for his signature. It is not up to me to say this, but I believe that the Supreme Command should have met before any directive is signed and agree with it by a show of hands, by voting, and then give it to the commander to sign. When the Supreme Commander signs it, the responsibility for the validity of the directive lies in the hands of the Supreme Command. The Supreme Command can then send the directive to the Main Staff in its entirety or he can send only its part to the Main Staff. Pursuant to what they receive from the Supreme Command, the Main Staff then issues their order, not directives but orders, and an order of the Main Staff goes for execution to the corps command. It is the Main Staff order rather than the directive that was signed by the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to one of these directives that you and I have talked about before. It's number 65 ter 29. It's dated 19 November 1992. It's known as directive operational number 4, and if we could go to -- let's just show you the first page of that so it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know why the Prosecution refers to the directive dated 19 November 1992. This is beyond the scope of the indictment. I believe that there are other directives that are more pertinent, more relevant for this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey? Unless you're going to offer Madam Fauveau to exchange seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can simply say that we -- as the indictment spells out and our trial brief spells out and I've said many times, this area is pertinent and an important part of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can proceed further by explaining the relevance that you attach to this document more specifically at least rather than generically as you have put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's actually mentioned in the indictment as part of the lead-up and the history of what culminated in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can stop there. That's what we had in mind, too, but you hadn't stated it. The witness can proceed to answer your question, please. General?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, yes, General, I just wanted you to see the first page so you can recognise the date and the title, and let's go to the -- I think it's the last page of the B/C/S version so we can see what that says. It may be the second to the last page. It says who it was drafted by. Can you tell us while we are getting to that, who drafted directive 4?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And was that in your capacity as Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to the Drina Corps section. Actually, it's paragraph -- it's numbered 5 in the B/C/S but it's 5D, and the part I want to ask you about is the part I've asked you about before, and if-- if we can get it to 5D so that -- page 10 of the B/C/S, if that will be helpful. Maybe we can blow up D so that it can be read a bit better. Not sure that's D. I think that's E, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There we go. And the -- I apologise. I hope the interpreters can read that. I'll just -- it's not long so I'll just say it, "The Drina Corps, from its present positions, its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad, the dam, Zvornik and the corridor, while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him, and force him to leave the Birac, Zepa and Gorazde areas." Now, I understand it, that's war, that's what war is all about, but let me ask you about this next comment. "Force him to leave the Birac, Zepa and Gorazde areas together with the Muslim population." Why did you write in this, "To force the Muslim population out"?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before the witness answers, could the Prosecutor read the entire paragraph just to put it in context, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Mr. McCloskey. I don't think you have an objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "Inflict heaviest possible losses on him and force him to leave the Birac, Zepa and Gorazde areas together with the Muslim population. First, offer the able-bodied and armed men to surrender, and if they refuse, destroy them. After that, unblock and repair the Konjevic Polje-Zvornik road, make it fit for traffic and stand by for intensive combat against infiltrated sabotage, terrorists, surprise and ambush attacks and paramilitary groups. Set up a command post in Vlasenica and a forward command post as decided by the corps commander." Now, I'm not asking you about this second section, about "offer the able-bodied and armed men to surrender and if they refuse, destroy them." But I would like to direct your attention to the part about "force him to leave Birac, Zepa and Gorazde areas together with the Muslim population." Why would you put in forcing out the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Prosecutor, sir, exactly 18 months ago, you kept me at a stage or in a position of anxiety over this text when you questioned me on that 18th of October in Banja Luka. You know that the text was not legible, the copy was very bad, just as it was now. But at that time, because I was unable to read it myself, you read it and the interpreter, Ms. Adisa, interpreted it as you read it to me, and I came away with the impression that what was written there was exhaust or wage a war of attrition with the civilian population. Now, when I heard it for the second time, I heard a G instead of N, so that it came as "izgoravite" [phoen] instead of "iznoravite," [phoen] which means push out, not exhaust. Now, the things I want to say now is that first of all, it is not said anywhere in this text, exhaust civilian population. It says exhaust the enemy, maximise his losses, and force him out, with the civilian -- with the Muslim population, the areas of Birac, Zepa and Gorazde. So the first thing that has to be clear is there is no attrition against the civilian population. Second, as the war began, and sometime into the war, let me say in the first third of the war, the entire population of all three ethnic groups started moving across Bosnia-Herzegovina. Serbs were withdrawing to areas with a majority Serb population for their own personal safety or they crossed over to Serbia. Muslims moved in three directions, sometimes under agreement, sometimes out of fear. One direction was into central Bosnia, just as with the Serbs, to places with a majority Muslim population. Another part moved out to third countries, European countries, Islamic countries, the US, Canada and so on. The poorer part of the population in Podrinje tended to move out into larger places like Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde. This directive is 15 years old. The objective was, once the civilian population moves out, to have no army left in that area, and it says, "Force able-bodied men to turn over their weapons." It doesn't say "capture," as you put it. Those who do not turn over their weapons, and intend to stay in the area, were to be destroyed. And I think that is perfectly all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you agree with me that this is a reference to forcing the civilian population from the area?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. It's about forcing armed units, that is troops, to move out from that civilian area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you explain the last section of that comment that says, "Force them to leave, together with the Muslim population"?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do not see that it means -- that it says force them out with. It says, "Force the enemy, with the Muslim population, to leave." So if the Muslim population is leaving, the troops should too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I had noticed you standing up, but you sat down again. That's why I didn't intervene. Okay, thank you. Go ahead, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, General, we had also talked briefly in Banja Luka about directive 7, which was dated 8 March 1995, and is 65 ter number 5, and perhaps we can save some time, but like your directive, at the end, it says, "Drafted by Colonel Radivoje Miletic." Do you have any reason to believe that it was not drafted by Colonel -- at the time Colonel Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no reason to believe one way or another. General Miletic is best placed to know whether he drafted it or not. I did not participate in the drafting of this directive. I was not familiar with it. And Miletic is the one who knows best whether he wrote it up or not, just as I told you that I wrote directive number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, at the end of the document, and we can go there if would you like -- if fact, we better, I think. It's number 5, 65 ter number 5, it's right at the end, and like your document, it says, "Drafted by" and we'll go to that so you can see it. Well, you can take a look at that document. It's the heading, and we'll get back to that a little bit later because we can see your name on that one, but I'll ask you about that later. If we could go to page 21 in the B/C/S. Just near the bottom there. And can you see, just above the stamp, it says, "Drafted by Colonel Radivoje Miletic, typed by Staff Sergeant Spasoja Zeljkovic" This is a pretty important document. Any reason to believe this would be a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: What could be a mistake? I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That they mistakenly put in General Miletic's name as the drafter.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I told you a moment ago, I have no reason to believe one way or another or to believe or disbelieve, because General Miletic is the one who knows best whether he wrote this directive or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said you didn't have anything to do with it earlier. And if we could go back to that first page that was shown, and this is -- appears to be some kind of a cover letter, the document itself -- all right. The letter I've got is page 23 in the B/C/S, and the cover letter is dated 17 March, where the actual directive is dated 8 March, and the cover letter, this particular one, is marked "very urgent, directive for upcoming operations to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps," and it says, "Enclosed with this document we are sending you the directive for further operations, number 7." And it says, "Confirm receipt of the above mentioned directive by returning a copy of this document." And it says, "Chief of Staff, Lieutenant General Manojlo Milovanovic." Is that your signature, if you can tell from this?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you at least were involved in sending this directive out to the 1st Krajina Corps, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So you had read this directive by the 17th of March, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I read it or not. I believe not. Because I write the accompanying letter with the directive that is sent to the corps command, which means the directive has already been signed, legally validated. I don't even know why it was sent to the corps. The corps should have received the order of the Main Staff proceeding from this. It's probably that I was around. This was probably sent by courier because it obviously didn't go by teletype, and even if I had read it, I would have been unable to change, modify anything in that directive. I wouldn't have dared to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why wouldn't you have dared to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't have dared to because it was signed by the Supreme Commander. I was not the author. I did not participate in any way in its drafting. And this cover letter is just giving authority to the courier to send it to the -- to take it, in fact, to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps and it's written here that the corps received it on the 21st of March, 1995, which means that the courier, the messenger, whoever took it there, took four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another document. This is 65 ter 2672, another one we had talked about, and oh, just to clear up, on directive 4, were you able -- I gave you copies of that last night. Were you able to read that copy I gave you last night, to be prepared today?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean directive number 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We just discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just want to make sure you were able to read that copy, because you said the one in Banja Luka, you were not able to read.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have managed to read it last night by combining all possible and impossible spectacles, combining desk lamps and somehow I managed to read it and that is why I opposed your suggestion that the text said something about exhausting or pushing out the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Here is another document that we had talked about before. It's dated 14 July, from the command of the 5th Engineering Battalion, and it's transmitted by courier, apparently. It's called a regular combat report. And it says, "The enemy." Now, before I read what it says and ask you about that, is it fair to say the 5th Engineering Battalion is part of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And they were located at this time in the area of Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where he was, but he was certainly in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps, maybe Konjevic Polje because that's where part of the -- where the part of the Protection Regiment was located, or maybe he was closer to Milici or in Bratunac, but it was certainly somewhere in that area, east of the Zvornik-Vlasenica-Han Pijesak road, on the Drina side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me read this to you. It says, "A large enemy group was infiltrated in the region of Pobrdje Brdo and the region of Konjevic Polje. Units of the 5th Engineering Battalion and the MUP successfully resisted the enemy. About 1.000 to 1500 enemy civilians and soldiers were arrested and killed." Now we talked about this before. Is there any justification to kill people after you arrest them?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there isn't. It's a war crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when I asked you last time whether or not you thought this could be a war crime, that's what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this regular combat report was sent -- it says it's sent to the Drina Corps. Is that part of its normal reporting chain, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a normal reporting chain because the 5th Engineering Battalion was an independent unit directly linked to the corps command, not to any of the brigade commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you had mentioned in one of your answers that you had come back to go to General Zivanovic's retirement function, and can you tell us what date you came back for that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, if you would be so kind, could you remove this because it's distracting me, unless we need it some more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, we don't, and I think that's a very good idea.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what date you came back to go to General Zivanovic's function?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said it's 19th and 20th. He said it already. He gave us the dates before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did do you when you came back on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I arrived at the Main Staff, the above-ground part of the barracks sometimes close to dark on the 19th. I didn't find anybody in the house, none of the officers. And I asked the duty person who was the most senior person around at the Main Staff, and he said General Gvero. So as a disciplined soldier I reported to General Gvero because he was the most senior in the staff automatically. I asked him where Mladic was, and General Gvero if I remember correctly said that Mladic was negotiating with somebody about Zepa and it was most likely that Serb forces would also go into Zepa. After that exchange, I went to sleep and I saw Gvero the next day, not only Gvero but all the people who had gathered to see General Zivanovic off, at the Jela restaurant. That's between Sokolac and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you reported to General Gvero on the 19th, was it in person or by telephone, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember. Maybe we talked in person. General Gvero is here. Maybe he can confirm. But we had that conversation, although I don't remember whether it was over the phone or in person. But I think it was in person, because Gvero had just come out of the bathroom. I probably wouldn't have that image in my mind if somebody had told it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you remember at the Jela restaurant the next day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic? 16

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just an answer, a bit of the answer missing. [Microphone not activated]. [In English] "I don't know," this part is missing from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I think now we've got more missing in the transcript of what you said. That's because you changed, switched from one language to the other. What is missing, Mr. Krgovic? As I understood to you say, it's that the witness had said it, I don't know, but where exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where did he say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the end -- it's line -- it's 73, number 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said, "I don't know" what? When you said, "I don't know," General, you still in other words are not certain whether you actually met him in person or whether you spoke to him on the phone or some other kind of communication or are you now sure that you met him in person and you're not sure, you don't know about something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have answered the Prosecutor's question, whether I contacted with Gvero in person or on the phone, and I answered to the Prosecutor, "I don't know" and that "I don't know" was not in the transcript because I just uttered it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey, we've got two minutes left, if they can serve you any purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have one little office diagram sketch. It won't take me very long but give than we don't want to crowd into the next case. It's not on e-court. It will be on the ELMO and I think we can do it quicker if we -- I'll just take five or ten minutes and I know my credibility on that score is not good today, but I won't take more than 10 minutes, I'm sure, if we start up tomorrow on this. One exhibit, that's the last area I want to ask him about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. General, we are going to adjourn today. We'll meet again tomorrow morning same time, hopefully earlier, 9.00, without any technical hitches, hopefully and we will continue. In the meantime, General, between now and tomorrow since you haven't finished your testimony, you're not to communicate or allow anyone to communicate with you to discuss or even mention the subject matter of your testimony, of the events that you're testifying upon. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Nice afternoon and evening, everyone.
